options.misconception: ties coverage to a legislative outcome

options.misconception: narrows the subject matters to introduced bills

options.text: Covered contacts are all conversations with any federal official on any topic
options.misconception: removes the subject-matter limit entirely

options.text: Covered contacts are those about federal legislation, taxes, licences, or loans and financial aid

options.text: The office manager, because anyone employed by a lobbying organisation is covered
options.misconception: treats all staff of a covered firm as lobbyists

options.text: None of them, because only elected officials can be lobbyists
options.misconception: inverts the definition entirely

options.misconception: assumes unpaid advocacy is registrable

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The income figure that exempts a registrant
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a spending threshold is a trigger rather than an exemption
questions.stem: A local newspaper is correcting its earlier claim that a small client can lobby freely below a spending threshold. Write the correction.

answer.exemplar: The figure the newspaper confused is a registration trigger, not an exemption. A client that spends more than 500,000 dollars on lobbying in a calendar year must register the lobbying firm that works for it, and the firm must register in turn, with a lower figure of 200,000 dollars for a state or local government client. Below the threshold the activity is not registered, but it is not thereby made lawful or free of the rules that apply to everyone.

questions.explanation: A spending threshold above which registration is compulsory does not create permission below which lobbying is unregulated. The correction must say the figure triggers registration, not an exemption.
questions.hint: Distinguish a registration trigger from an exemption.

questions.topic: The honest-broker account of organised interests
questions.learningObjective: State what the broker account claims organised interests do

stimulus.body: A lecturer told a civic audience that organised interests are best understood as brokers who gather private demands, reconcile the conflicts between them and carry the resulting, more moderate package to government, which is why they are described as a working part of the political system rather than a distortion of it.

questions.stem: Taking the lecturer's account as the thing being explained, which statement best describes it?

options.text: It treats organised interests as buyers of influence who purchase decisions they could not obtain on merit
options.misconception: replaces the account with a venal view

options.text: It claims that organised interests are illegal because they trade influence for support
options.misconception: assumes the account is a legal objection

options.text: It argues that organised interests have no influence because politics is decided elsewhere
options.misconception: recasts the account as a denial of influence

options.text: It treats organised interests as aggregators that filter and reconcile demands for government

questions.explanation: The broker account emphasises aggregation: groups take private demands, filter and combine them, and present a workable set to officials. That is why organised interests count as part of the system.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The collective-action problem in group formation
questions.learningObjective: Explain the collective-action problem in a concrete case

stimulus.body: A village meeting drew nine people who all said they wanted the stream kept clean, and the list of tasks to do it named forty households. Two people said they would help only if their own driveway were cleared first, and none of the others came back.

questions.stem: From that note, which correction should the committee make to its earlier belief?

options.text: The committee was right to expect help, because the interest is clearly shared
options.misconception: assumes a common interest guarantees cooperation

options.text: The committee was wrong to expect help, because nine people are too few to matter
options.misconception: judges the group by size alone

options.text: The committee should have expected free riding, because shared benefits weaken the incentive to join
The committee should have recruited more volunteers, because larger groups always act
options.misconception: assumes bigger groups organise more easily

questions.explanation: When benefits are shared and non-excludable, each person gains from the group's success while bearing only their own cost, so many will not contribute. Groups answer this with selective incentives.
questions.hint: Ask why each person had little reason to show up.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Clienteliage and the exchange of help for loyalty
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes an exchange clientelistic rather than programmatic
questions.stem: A debate team is preparing a correction of the common error that any exchange of help for support is the same thing. Write their briefing.

answer.exemplar: Clienteliage is a particular kind of exchange: a patron or broker provides individualised assistance, such as a job, a permit or a favour, and receives in return the loyalty of the person helped, who votes for the patron and discourages others from defecting. It differs from programmatic support, where a voter backs a party or programme because of its policies and receives benefits that go to a whole group, and the difference matters for accountability, because a personal vote can be bought.

questions.explanation: The correction must hold two ideas apart: an exchange of help for loyalty, and support for a programme whose benefits are shared. The first is clientelism and weakens accountability.
questions.hint: Distinguish individualised help from shared benefits.

options.misconception: takes a side without stating the objection

questions.explanation: The elitist objection targets the inference, not the existence of groups: a crowded field of organised interests may still leave decisions to a few, and agenda setting matters too.

options.misconception: explains the drift by character

options.text: The drift follows from division of labour, expertise and control of information as the group grows

options.misconception: blames members rather than structure

questions.learningObjective: Explain why support work is covered by the statute
questions.stem: A teaching group wants to correct the common belief that only the conversations count. Write the explanation for their handout.

answer.exemplar: The statute is wider than the visible meetings. Efforts include advocacy on behalf of a client, lobbying itself, research, analysis or other assistance designed to support lobbying activities, and any communication with a covered official on behalf of a client. So the analyst who prepares the briefing that shapes what a lobbyist says in the room, and the assistant who drafts the letters, are doing covered work even though neither ever picks up the telephone to an official.

questions.explanation: Support work is covered because the statute defines efforts to include research and analysis designed to support lobbying activities. The visible call is only the part most people think about.

options.text: No correction is needed, because the firm registered in an earlier year
options.misconception: treats an old registration as a current one

options.misconception: accepts any filing date as timely

Organised interests exist to defeat the preferences of the wider public

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The collective-action problem in group formation
questions.learningObjective: Explain why shared interests do not produce organisation
questions.stem: A mutual aid group's officers are correcting the belief that members will organise themselves once the problem becomes clear. Write the correction for their members' handbook.

answer.exemplar: The correction is about incentives rather than information. When the benefit of an action is shared by everyone while its cost falls on whoever performs it, each member is better off letting others do the work, and if everyone reasons that way the group provides little or nothing. That is why groups that do form often attach selective incentives, such as a service, a discount or a benefit that only participants receive, and why narrow interests organise more readily than broad ones.

questions.explanation: The problem is not ignorance but the structure of the payoff, because individual rationality produces collective inaction. Selective incentives and narrow interests are the usual escapes.
questions.hint: Show why each member's calculation defeats the group.

questions.stem: A newspaper is preparing to correct its earlier framing of organised interests, and asks you to write the account it should print instead.

answer.exemplar: Organised interests, on this account, are brokers rather than just pressure. The account does not claim that brokers are neutral, and the usual objection is that they tend to carry the preferences of the better organised rather than the general interest.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The argument that organisations drift toward leadership control
questions.learningObjective: Set out the structural account of drift toward control
questions.stem: A student union is correcting the belief that its officers took control deliberately. Write the structural account for its handbook.

answer.exemplar: The classic argument is that control concentrates in growing democratic organisations whatever the intentions of the people in it. As membership grows, work is divided and specialisation follows, so some members acquire knowledge and handle the records and correspondence; others become dependent on them for information and cannot easily check what is done; and incumbency adds to this, because the few in office control the organisation's resources and its contacts. The result is described as an iron law of oligarchy, a tendency that strong democratic commitments do not prevent.

questions.explanation: The explanation concerns incentives and information, not leaders' characters. Division of labour, expertise, control of records and incumbency make concentration likely even in democratic groups.
questions.hint: Explain the mechanisms rather than the motives.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a threshold figure is not a safe harbour
questions.stem: An association's treasurer asks you to write the guidance that corrects the belief that a threshold figure is a safe harbour. Write it.

answer.exemplar: The figures in the statute are triggers, not safe harbours. An organisation whose gross income exceeds 3,000,000 dollars and which meets the hours or spending test must register, and a client that spends more than 500,000 dollars on lobbying in a year, or more than 200,000 dollars where the client is a state or local government, must register the firm that works for it. questions.explanation: A threshold defines when a filing duty begins, and nothing in the statute suggests that staying below it licenses conduct the law forbids. Guidance should say a lighter burden is not a permission.
questions.hint: Say what the figure triggers rather than what it permits.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The pluralism and elitist disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Write the disagreement between the two accounts
questions.stem: A seminar wants a written statement of the disagreement between the pluralist and elitist accounts. Write it.

answer.exemplar: The pluralist account holds that many groups compete in an open political system, that no single group dominates, and that the number of competing interests makes concentrated domination unlikely. The elitist objection holds that the appearance of many groups conceals a much smaller effective elite, that institutional arrangements such as closed decision making give that elite a decisive advantage, and that many apparent conflicts of interest never reach the agenda at all. The dispute is therefore about who really sets outcomes, and it is settled by evidence of influence rather than by counting groups.

questions.explanation: The account on one side says many competing groups diffuse power, and the objection says the visible competition conceals a small elite whose preferences survive. Both make claims about outcomes.
questions.hint: Set the two claims about outcomes against each other.

answer.exemplar: The statute works with two ideas. options.misconception: treats combination as failure

options.text: The groups succeeded in blocking government, since fewer demands were heard
options.misconception: reads a reduction as obstruction

questions.explanation: The broker account expects this: overlapping demands are filtered and combined, so many groups can present officials with a smaller workable set. The finding is evidence of aggregation, not failure.
questions.hint: Ask what the reduction in demands shows about aggregation.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The collective-action problem in group formation
questions.learningObjective: Identify the step that changes the incentive to join
questions.stem: A diagram traces a group's formation: a shared interest is identified, each member assumes others will act, no one volunteers, and later a benefit is offered only to those who join. Which arrow marks the step the argument treats as decisive?

options.text: The step where the members-only benefit appears, because it changes the private payoff
The step where the shared interest is identified, because information is what was missing
options.misconception: explains the outcome by information rather than incentives

options.text: The step where each member assumes others will act, because the assumption is irrational
options.misconception: blames the reasoning of members

options.text: The step where the group finally forms, because formation is the end of the story
options.misconception: treats the outcome as the explanation

questions.explanation: The decisive step is the selective incentive, because it changes what each member personally gains from joining and removes the reason to wait. Identifying the interest does not change the payoff.
questions.hint: Ask which step changes what a member personally gains.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Clienteliage and the exchange of help for loyalty
questions.learningObjective: Explain how clientelage differs from programmatic politics
questions.stem: A local history class is correcting the belief that any benefit handed out by a politician is corruption. Write the explanation they want.

answer.exemplar: Clientelage is not simply the giving of benefits. It is a relationship in which a patron, often working through brokers, provides individualised help to a particular person or family and receives in return that person's loyalty at the ballot box and their influence over others. A programme that improves services for a whole district, or a rule that treats everyone alike, is not clientelage even though politicians may claim credit for it, and the distinction matters because clientelage buys personal votes and weakens the accountability that programmatic politics provides.

questions.explanation: The test is the personal return, not the mere existence of a benefit. Individualised help for loyalty is clientelage, whereas shared benefits are programmatic and can be judged on their merits.
questions.hint: Ask whether the benefit produced personal loyalty.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The pluralism and elitist disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Compute the concentration of contacts across agencies
questions.stem: A survey records 200 contacts between organised groups and agencies and finds that 150 of them went to 5 agencies. What percentage of contacts were concentrated in those 5 agencies?
questions.explanation: Divide concentrated contacts by the total: 150 divided by 200 equals 0.75, or 75 percent. Concentration of attention is the pattern the elitist objection points to, though it proves no control.
questions.hint: Divide the concentrated contacts by the total contacts.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The argument that organisations drift toward leadership control
questions.learningObjective: Apply the structural account to an organisation's history

stimulus.body: A union's membership grew from 300 to 1,500 over twenty years. The note records that day-to-day decisions came to be made by a small committee, that the committee kept the membership's records, and that the branch presidents who once attended every meeting stopped coming.

questions.stem: Reading the union's note, which correction should its history carry?

options.text: The drift reflects the personal ambition of the committee members
options.misconception: explains the outcome by character rather than structure

options.text: The drift matches the structural argument, because specialisation and records concentrate control
The drift has nothing to do with size, because membership is irrelevant to the argument
options.misconception: denies the role of organisational growth

options.text: The drift shows that the members lost interest, which is the real cause
options.misconception: blames members' apathy rather than the design

questions.explanation: Growth, division of labour, control of records and members withdrawing from meetings are all mechanisms in the structural argument, so the history illustrates it without needing bad intentions.
questions.hint: Ask which structural mechanisms the note records.
